candidates.attacker_control: Values that reach message parameters can be attacker-influenced: the public API `HibernateConstraintValidatorContext.addMessageParameter(String, Object)` (ConstraintValidatorContextImpl lines 106-116) is intended for custom validators to insert arbitrary values (commonly the validated value) into messages, and built-in `UniqueElementsValidator` inserts strings derived from the validated collection's duplicate elements (`duplicates`, lines 55-59). The validated value itself is also attacker-controlled and is bound as the `validatedValue` EL variable (ElTermResolver lines 84-88). Any application pattern that reflects such data through a `{name}` placeholder (e.g. message `"{value} is invalid"` with `addMessageParameter("value", input)`, or a custom `@UniqueElements(message = "duplicates: {duplicates}")`) makes the injected `${...}` string attacker-controlled.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: EL support in messages is a documented feature, so developer-authored `${...}` in a message template is intended behavior; the issue is specifically EL introduced via substituted parameter values. The repository already ships `InterpolationHelper.escapeMessageParameter` and uses it in PatternValidator/AbstractScriptAssertValidator, showing the project's own mitigation pattern is only applied to two known parameters, not centrally. Default built-in messages do not place user-derived strings into parameters other than `{duplicates}` (not referenced by the default UniqueElements message) and `{regexp}`/`{script}` (explicitly escaped), so the default `@Pattern`/`@ScriptAssert` paths are mitigated; exploitation therefore depends on an application template that references an untrusted parameter. `ParameterMessageInterpolator` (lines 29-38) does not evaluate EL and is not affected. EL results are inserted as literal tokens (TokenIterator:69-73), so evaluation is not recursive within a pass; the flaw is the cross-pass re-tokenization after parameter substitution. I could not inspect the upstream fix/patched version or any CVE/patch metadata (not present in the snapshot), so the exact vulnerability-to-CVE mapping remains unverified.
candidates.impact: Attacker-shaped EL expressions are evaluated during violation-message interpolation. In the exposed EL context, bean property access and (implementation-dependent) method invocation on bound objects are possible, so impact ranges from disclosure of object state to invocation of arbitrary methods and, with common EL implementations, to code execution. At minimum it is improper neutralization of special elements in an expression language statement. This is a source-level lead; no runtime confirmation was performed.
candidates.prerequisites: (1) Default `ResourceBundleMessageInterpolator` is in use (it is the default: ConfigurationImpl line 472-475) so EL interpolation is enabled and a `javax.el` implementation is on the classpath; (2) the violation message template references a message parameter whose value carries attacker-controlled text; (3) the attacker can submit a value containing an EL expression (e.g. `${...}`). `ParameterMessageInterpolator` users are not affected. No authentication-specific precondition beyond the ability to submit the validated data.
candidates.root_cause: `AbstractMessageInterpolator.interpolateMessage` performs two sequential passes: step 2 resolves `{param}` message parameters, and step 3 then builds a brand-new `TokenIterator` (and `TokenCollector` of type EL) over the *result* of step 2 (lines 271-286). `ParameterTermResolver.interpolate` returns the parameter value as `variable.toString()` with no escaping (lines 24-40), so any `${...}` substring contained in a parameter value becomes an EL token in step 3 and is evaluated by `ElTermResolver` via `ExpressionFactory.createValueExpression(...).getValue(...)` (lines 61-80). The EL context is a `SimpleELContext` whose resolver chain ends in `BeanELResolver(true)` (lines 24-33), i.e. bean property access and method invocation are permitted (only `RootResolver.invoke` restricts the `formatter` base). Escaping of EL metacharacters exists (`InterpolationHelper.escapeMessageParameter`, lines 29-34) but is applied only locally by `PatternValidator` (line 46/56) and `AbstractScriptAssertValidator` (line 35), not to message parameters in general.
candidates.title: Expression-language injection through interpolated message parameters in AbstractMessageInterpolator
candidates.trace: User input -> validated bean value / custom validator -> `HibernateConstraintValidatorContext.addMessageParameter` (ConstraintValidatorContextImpl:106-116) -> ConstraintViolationCreationContext messageParameters -> ValidationContext.interpolate (lines 451-468) builds MessageInterpolatorContext with those parameters -> AbstractMessageInterpolator.interpolateMessage step 2 resolves `{name}` through ParameterTermResolver (24-40, unescaped toString) -> step 3 re-tokenizes the substituted string with InterpolationTermType.EL (lines 280-285; TokenCollector/ELState mark `${...}` as EL tokens) -> ResourceBundleMessageInterpolator.interpolate (74-77) -> InterpolationTerm -> ElTermResolver evaluates the expression with validatedValue/attributes/expression variables bound (82-105) in a SimpleELContext exposing BeanELResolver (SimpleELContext:24-33).
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed; no tests or fix commits are present in the assigned snapshot. Whether a given javax.el implementation allows method invocation (e.g. getClass()/Class.forName chains) through BeanELResolver was not verified here, and the real exploitability depends on the application referencing an untrusted message parameter. The precise upstream fix (escaping in ParameterTermResolver vs TokenIterator vs pass reordering) is inferred from the code's own mitigation pattern, not from a patch.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-917 (Expression Language Injection), potentially leading to CWE-94 (code injection) depending on the EL implementation

summary: Assigned snapshot is Hibernate Validator 6.0.17.Final (root pom.xml line 13; changelog ends at 6.0.17.Final) comprising 844 files (engine, cdi, annotation-processor, test-utils, performance). I focused on the message-interpolation pipeline, where the library evaluates Unified EL expressions contained in constraint-violation messages. The strongest source-backed lead is an expression-language injection path: message-parameter values are substituted first and then the whole interpolated string is re-tokenized and evaluated as EL, so a `${...}` sequence introduced through an untrusted parameter value is executed as an EL expression. The project itself contains a targeted mitigation for two validators (`InterpolationHelper.escapeMessageParameter`, used only in `PatternValidator` and `AbstractScriptAssertValidator`), which is not applied centrally to parameter substitution. Other reviewed areas (StAX XML config parsing, JSR-223 ScriptAssert, SafeHtml/jsoup-based validation) produced weaker or unconfirmed leads and are listed as rejected.
